abstract: We measure investors’ short- and long-term stock-return expectations using both options and survey data. These expectations at different horizons reveal what investors think their own short-term expectations will be in the future, or forward return expectations. Across data sources, investors’ forward return expectations are countercyclical, especially when measured as forward risk premiums. This countercyclical variation is, however, excessive, as changes in forward return expectations are too large relative to subsequent realized short-term expectations. The excess variation in forward return expectations can help account for a meaningful share of the stock-price declines during the global financial crisis and the COVID-19 crisis. (JEL G10, G12, G40)
title: Forward Return Expectations

abstract: We decompose cross-sectional differences in the level of price-earnings ratios using professional forecasts. High price-earnings ratios are accounted for by both low expected returns and overly high expected earnings growth. The magnitudes and timing of the comovements between prices, earnings growth, and returns are consistent with gradual learning rather than expectations being highly sensitive to recent realizations. Earnings growth surprises do not translate 1-1 into one-period returns but instead are gradually reflected in returns over time. A structural risk-premium model incorporating constant-gain learning about mean earnings growth replicates our findings and generates realistic dispersion and persistence in price-earnings ratios. (JEL G11, G12, G14, G40)
title: The Cross-section of Subjective Expectations: Understanding Prices and Anomalies

abstract: We estimate the supply-side effects of climate change on firm sales by exploiting variation in local average temperature across suppliers of the same client. A 1°C increase in temperature leads to a 2.5% decline in annual sales. This effect is nonlinear, with stronger effects among suppliers in regions with the largest temperature increases and in cooler regions. Manufacturing and heat-sensitive industries are more affected, consistent with a reduction in labor productivity and labor supply when local temperatures rise. Nondiversified and financially constrained firms are also more affected, supporting the importance of operational and financial flexibility in adapting to climate change.
journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis
title: Does Climate Change Affect Firm Sales? Identifying Supply Effects

abstract: Using regression discontinuity and difference-in-differences designs to compare prices of California homes across a new wildfire risk zone boundary, I identify null effects in the immediate vicinity of the new risk zone boundary. In contrast, prices of homes newly assigned to a riskier zone drop by 5.7% further away from the new risk zone boundary. These findings suggest that households do not respond to the risk salience triggered by the new risk zone assignment. Instead, they update their risk beliefs in response to rezoning in a way that is consistent with the actual wildfire risk.
journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis
title: Does the Salience of Climate-Related Risk Affect Asset Prices?

abstract: Initial sequence estimators are commonly used to estimate Monte Carlo standard errors for reversible Markov chains used in Markov chain Monte Carlo simulations. Despite their widespread use and subsequent methodological extensions, they are known only to be asymptotically conservative, with consistency still an open question. We address this gap by investigating the statistical properties of the initial positive sequence estimator. Leveraging a nonnegativity property of sums of adjacent autocovariances from reversible Markov chains, the initial positive sequence estimator is obtained by summing sample autocovariances until a sum of adjacent sample autocovariances becomes negative. We characterize the convergence behavior of this random truncation point. We also propose an alternative initial sequence type estimator based on a modified truncation rule. For both estimators, we establish consistency and derive bounds on rates of convergence, showing that, under geometric ergodicity, both converge to the asymptotic variance no slower than the near-parametric rate of (log n)/n 1/2. Finally, through empirical studies using both simulated and real-world data, we validate our theoretical findings and compare the empirical performance of the two initial sequence-type estimators with the standard overlapping batch mean estimator.
title: Consistency and convergence rate bounds of initial sequence type variance estimators for reversible Markov chains

abstract: Life‐cycle wage growth varies substantially across countries. We study the firm productivity distribution's role in a random‐search model with learning and labor‐market frictions, estimated for Brazil, Colombia, and the United States. Brazil has a long left tail of low‐paying firms, and Colombia has a highly compressed firm ladder. Replacing each country's firm distribution with that of the United States closes most of the cross‐country gap in wage growth, raising Brazil's relative wage growth from 73 to 103 percent and Colombia's from 52 to 115 percent. The results are robust to alternative distributional assumptions and additional sensitivity checks.
title: Life‐Cycle Wage Growth and Firm Productivity in Developed and Developing Economies

abstract: Why do recycling industries emerge rapidly in some resource markets but remain persistently marginal in others, even when recycling technologies are economically feasible? This paper develops a dynamic model of an exhaustible-resource monopolist interacting with a competitive fringe of recycling firms to examine how resource endowments shape the emergence of secondary supply. The model incorporates an endogenous waste stock: current extraction creates future recyclable waste, thereby affecting both the future scale of secondary supply and its entry conditions. We show that abundant reserves can induce the extractor to sustain a high-extraction path that deters recycling entry through limit pricing, generating prolonged dependence on virgin material supply. By contrast, when endowments are limited, continued extraction more rapidly erodes scarcity rents, reducing the incentive for exclusion and leading the extractor to accommodate secondary supply earlier. The analysis characterizes the resulting equilibrium transitions between virgin extraction and recycling. It thereby identifies a distinct deterrence mechanism: whereas related models may delay recycling by slowing depletion or waste accumulation, an incumbent can instead expand extraction to keep prices sufficiently low to deter secondary entry.
title: Recycling, endowments, and market power in exhaustible resource industries

abstract: This paper examines how reserve-backed stablecoins influence Treasury markets and financial intermediation. Using high-frequency Ethereum blockchain data matched to intraday returns on the BIL ETF that tracks short-term U.S. Treasuries, I show that large Tether issuances are followed by an increase in BIL prices in the following hour, reflecting a combination of forward-looking market expectations of sustained Treasury demand and Tether’s reserve deployment into short-term Treasuries. A complementary daily frequency analysis corroborates this pattern. A quantitative macro-finance model with capital-constrained banks and stablecoin issuers embeds this Treasury demand channel and reveals nonlinear amplification as the sector expands, highlighting how stablecoin growth can reshape safe asset pricing, bank balance sheets, and financial stability.
journal: Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control
title: Macro-Financial Impact of Stablecoin’s Demand for Treasuries

abstract: Growth in trade of perishable foods has significantly increased global access to fresh foods, but important trade-offs arising from perishability are not captured in standard trade models. In this paper, we develop a model of age-related product freshness that places importer logistics choices at the center of the analysis. The model highlights order size and order frequency as key trade margins, alongside the nonlinear pricing that arises from scale economies in trade. Importers determine freshness through their order-size and order-frequency choices, balancing a cost–quality trade-off. This has important implications for understanding the quality effects of growth, innovation, and trade policy. For instance, while innovations in cold-chain technology directly improve freshness, their overall effect depends on importers’ logistics choices, which also influence the carbon emissions associated with perishable trade. Fresh seafood is one of the most successful categories in the global expansion of fresh food trade. Using transaction-level data on Norwegian seafood exports from the world’s largest exporter of fresh seafood, we document that order-size discounts are important. We use the model to evaluate how reductions in perishability and protective tariffs affect trade outcomes and product freshness.
title: Logistics and product quality in perishable food trade

abstract: We present a two-sector growth model in which a representative agent invests in fossil fuel-based energy and renewable energy. These differ in capital intensity and project duration: fossil investments have lower upfront costs and more front-loaded payoffs; clean investments are more capital-intensive and have longer cost-recovery periods. We show that a negative economic shock (such as an energy supply shock or recession) leads to both cuts in total investment and to a shift in the composition of the remaining investment toward fossil fuel projects. This delays the clean energy transition, even if renewable energy is cost-effective on a levelised cost basis, implying a role for policies to sustain clean investment during recessions. We discuss how this mechanism can be amplified by higher interest rates, pro-cyclical climate policies, perceived risk, and financial frictions.
journal: Journal of Environmental Economics and Management
title: Energy shocks and the climate transition

abstract: US Treasuries have long been the benchmark dollar safe asset, and the convenience yield they command is the price the world pays for dollar liquidity. This column shows that the convenience yield on ten-year Treasuries relative to corporate bonds has collapsed from around 60 to 10 basis points since 2019, while the premium on repo has held near 90. Repo, not the Treasury, is now the highest-convenience dollar safe asset. The same shift helps explain why the dollar has been losing ground as the global reserve asset even as domestic convenience yields hold up.
title: Repo is the new dollar safe asset

abstract: In international affairs, what a country does depends on its own interests and on what its partners do. This column uses data on political institutions and UN voting to recover the network of geopolitical influence. The network tracks major shifts in international politics since the 1960s and reveals three notions of power: autonomy, control, and the ability to shape the game. Across all countries, the US has the most autonomy but China has the most control. Domestic political change in the US or China moves other countries the most, as the network transmits it furthest.
authors: Ernest Liu, Bennett Smith-Worthington, Stephen Redding, David Yang

title: A network approach to geopolitics

abstract: Reliable electricity supply is essential for firms to maintain production continuity and efficiency. Using daily newspaper text, we construct a city-level Electricity Supply Reliability Index (ESR) for China and match city-year electricity conditions to firm-level data from the National Tax Survey during 2009–2015. We find that a one-standard-deviation decrease in ESR is associated with an approximately 0.97% decline in firm total factor productivity (TFP). The relationship holds across a range of robustness tests. We further document two dimensions of structural adjustment. First, output and intermediate inputs become relatively more concentrated in cities with more reliable electricity supply. Second, deteriorating ESR is associated with greater within-industry differentiation: a one-standard-deviation decrease in ESR is associated with an approximately 0.16-percentage-point increase in the industry revenue share of firms in the top 10% of the operating-revenue distribution and a 0.003-percentage-point decrease in that of firms in the bottom 10%. Moreover, lower ESR is associated with lower TFP among follower firms, whereas the corresponding estimate for profit-defined industry leaders is statistically insignificant. These findings indicate that unreliable electricity supply is associated not only with lower average productivity but also with differences in the spatial distribution of production and firm performance within industries.

title: Electricity supply reliability and firm productivity: A dual perspective on spatial reallocation and within-industry differentiation

abstract: It is now well established that the COVID-19 pandemic had a devastating and unequal impact on student achievement. Test score declines were disproportionately large for historically marginalized students, exacerbating preexisting achievement gaps. In this paper, we use longitudinal student-level NWEA MAP Growth test data to estimate differences in test score declines for students at different points on the prepandemic test distribution. We examine whether these widening gaps occurred within schools and districts – between high- and low-achieving students – or between schools and districts that served more versus fewer lower-achieving students before the pandemic. We find that while lower-achieving students experienced greater incidence of learning loss during the pandemic (relative to higher-achieving peers), these differences are significantly attenuated with the inclusion of school and district fixed effects. Decomposition analyzes show that roughly three-quarters of the widening in math achievement occurred between schools, indicating that students with lower prior achievement disproportionately attended schools where average losses were larger.
title: Pandemic learning loss by student baseline achievement: extent and sources of heterogeneity

abstract: This paper sets forth a tractable incomplete markets monetary model with money and other nominal safe assets including a long-maturity government bond. Money serves as a medium of exchange whereas all safe assets allow agents to self-insure against risks. Portfolio demand for these assets can serve as a nominal anchor that determines the price level. The paper examines and contrasts monetary transmission mechanisms involving different monetary policy instruments and links it to classic monetary results, including the Tobin effect, Sims’ stepping on a rake effect, Sargent-Wallace unpleasant monetarist arithmetic, Wallace neutrality of open market operations, and the Friedman rule.
journal: Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control
title: A Monetary Model with Money and Safe Assets

abstract: We study how the precision with which merger-specific efficiencies are assessed affects the incentives to invest in such efficiencies before the merger review. With binary investment and an exogenous cutoff, greater precision strengthens investment incentives. We then show how the analysis extends to continuous investment choice and Bayesian approval. A more rigorous merger assessment can therefore encourage efficiency creation.
title: Merger control and investment: The role of efficiency assessment

abstract: How can an institutional shock alter the economic value of productive capabilities? The shock can change the viability of activities in which capabilities are deployed, shifting derived demand and revaluing those capabilities. Capabilities are more exposed to revaluation when their economic value depends more strongly on the affected institutional conditions, while revaluation is amplified by high activity substitutability and low capability transferability. Demand shifts can generate labor-market disequilibrium when established deployment contracts faster than alternative productive capacity can expand. Adverse capability revaluation can also make institutions themselves an object of adjustment. Agents facing larger losses, limited labor-adjustment opportunities, and greater institutional-adjustment capacity are more likely to seek institutional restoration or modification. Institutional shocks can therefore set in motion a recursive process: they revalue capabilities and reorganize labor markets, while the resulting gains and losses create incentives for endogenous institutional adjustment.
title: Institutional Shocks and Capability Revaluation: Labor-Market Disequilibrium and Endogenous Institutional Adjustment
